title: The Main Story: One Router Grounded America, and Washington Wired It That Way
dek: A box in El Dorado, Arkansas may have stopped every departing flight in the country. The reason it could is copper from the 1960s, money that arrives in drips and drabs, and a lot of blaming whoever had the job last.
body:
## One Router to Rule Them All

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration did something it has done only a handful of times in a generation: it stopped every departing flight in the United States. The nationwide ground stop lasted more than four hours, and the FAA cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." [1] It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 and only the second since the September 11 attacks, [3] and it disrupted roughly 15,000 flights across Friday and Saturday. [3] Planes already in the air were allowed to land, and international flights were handled case by case; [1] the most powerful aviation system on Earth had, briefly, become a very large parking lot.

And what took it down? Not a hostile nation. Not a hacker in a hoodie. According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's preliminary account, a router. [2] A contractor working for L3Harris was switching copper wire to fiber at a remote FAA site, replacing a router, and the new box began flooding other routers with about 1,000 login attempts every four to five seconds. [2] The first device sat at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and Duffy said a second router, installed about three weeks earlier in Amarillo, Texas, "started to flood our system as well." [4]

El Dorado. The legendary lost city of gold, which explorers spent centuries failing to find, turns out to have been hiding one networking appliance capable of scrambling an entire American Friday. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said 50,000 flights were scheduled that day and about 12,000 were not completed. [2]

Now, to be fair to the router: we don't know yet whether it was the router. Bedford said the review will determine whether the device was installed or configured incorrectly, or was simply defective, and Juniper's owner, HPE, says its devices "did not fail." [4] Duffy himself put it as "the installation or the router that was the bad actor." [3] So, as of this writing, the official suspect list is: a box, or the people who plugged in the box. Investigators have seen no evidence of a cyberattack. [4]

But here's the thing. Whatever the root cause turns out to be, the reason one remote site in southern Arkansas could knock over the entire country is not a mystery at all. It's been written down, in detail, by government auditors, for years.

## How We Got Here: A Brief History of "Next Year"

Let's start with the copper. The Government Accountability Office reported in September that the FAA's telecommunications "copper cables are from the 1960s," using technology providers no longer support. [5] The FAA plans to replace 5,170 copper lines with fiber, and as of May 2026 it had replaced 2,560 of them. [5] That's not a modernization program; that's a coin flip.

Duffy, to his credit, did not pretend otherwise. "We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines," he said after the outage. [1] On Fox News Sunday he said the FAA is "still using an old 1980 architecture for telecom." [3] If your air traffic control network were a person, it would now be old enough to have opinions about how music was better before.

The copper is only the most recent chapter. A 2024 GAO review, cited in the September report, rated 51 of the FAA's 138 air traffic control systems, 37 percent, as unsustainable, and another 54 as potentially unsustainable. [5] And before the current overhaul there was NextGen, the modernization program that was supposed to be finished by 2025. The FAA spent more than $14 billion on it from fiscal 2007 through 2022, its projected cost through 2030 is at least $35 billion, and GAO said the FAA didn't expect to finish until at least 2030. [5] NextGen is the only "next generation" in history that has been next for three presidential administrations and counting.

And the warning lights have been blinking. In January 2023, under the Biden administration, a "damaged database file" in the NOTAM pilot-alert system triggered a nationwide pause on domestic departures; thousands of flights were delayed. [9] In May 2025, under the Trump administration, radar screens at the facility handling Newark went dark for about 90 seconds, the second such outage in weeks, which the FAA blamed on a "telecommunications outage." [10] Different parties, different presidents, same plot: the system falls over, everyone says "unacceptable," and the cables stay copper.

## The Money: A Story in Drips and Drabs

So surely the problem is that nobody will pay for it? Well. Partly.

In July 2025 Congress appropriated $12.5 billion for the FAA's new air traffic control overhaul, which the agency calls the Brand New Air Traffic Control System. [5] (Yes, "Brand New." The previous one was "Next." At this rate the 2040 version will be called "Seriously, This Time.") The FAA projects the first phase will cost $10.6 billion and says the second phase needs about $10.2 billion more. [5]

After Friday, Duffy called for $50 billion in upgrades. [1] President Trump blamed his predecessor, calling it a Biden-era "FAA disaster" and writing that the work "should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs." [8] Which, honestly, is the most correct sentence anyone has said about this system in years. Hold that thought.

Because the Democrats on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee came back with a number of their own. Fifteen months after Congress approved the $12.5 billion, they said, the administration has obligated $4.3 billion and spent $1 billion, leaving "$8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent." [6] Their question, roughly: why ask for more when you haven't spent what you've got? [6] Duffy's answer is that the existing money was designated for radar, radios and electronic flight strips, not a new communications network. [3]

So the drips are coming from the faucet, and both sides are arguing about who's holding the bucket.

There's also the matter of Duffy's own voting record, which critics dug up within hours. In 2019, as a congressman, he voted against H.R. 267, a transportation and housing spending bill introduced during the 35-day shutdown that included FAA money. [7] PolitiFact rated the claim that he "voted against upgrading air traffic control systems" Mostly False, noting he voted for FAA funding and reauthorization bills in 2012, 2014 and 2018. [7] So: not the smoking gun his critics want. But it does capture the deeper problem perfectly. FAA money in this country rides along on whatever must-pass spending bill is lurching through Congress, and it gets held hostage with everything else.

## The Hostage Situation

Which brings us to the part nobody in Washington likes to say out loud: the agency that keeps planes apart is funded the way you'd fund a book club.

Look at last fall. On day 38 of the 2025 government shutdown, the FAA ordered a 10 percent cut in air traffic at the country's 40 largest airports, and the agency acknowledged that "controllers have been working without pay." [11] Think about that. The people whose job is to stop two aircraft from occupying the same piece of sky were being asked to do it while wondering how to cover rent.

And there aren't enough of them. The FAA had about 11,000 certified controllers as of April 2026, against a target of 12,563, and a January 2026 GAO analysis found the U.S. has about 6 percent fewer controllers than a decade ago while flights relying on the system grew 10 percent. [12] The agency did hire 2,235 controller trainees in fiscal 2026, its most ever, [12] which is genuinely good news, and also the kind of good news you get when you have to dig out of a very deep hole.

Who benefits from all this? Not passengers, who paid in missed weddings and airport-floor naps. Not controllers. The honest answer is: politicians, who get a fresh disaster to blame on the other team every few years. In 2023, it was the Democrats' problem. In 2025, it was the Republicans' problem. This weekend it was Biden's problem, according to the president, [8] and the administration's problem, according to House Democrats. [6] Everyone wins the press release. Nobody wins the fiber.

## The Questions Nobody Has Answered

There are a few things about Friday that deserve real answers, and soon.

First: why was critical network work happening on a Friday afternoon? A Washington Examiner reporter said on CNN that the roughly 60 controllers she'd spoken with weren't buying the official explanation, and that this kind of work usually happens "midweek, middle of the night." [13] That's secondhand, from unnamed controllers, so treat it as a question rather than a finding. But it's a good question.

Second: where was the redundancy? Ron Bartsch, an aviation academic, told Al Jazeera, "The whole aviation community is based on redundancy." [1] A system that can be toppled by one site is, by definition, not very redundant.

Third: was anyone managing the overlap? GAO warned in September that the FAA has no integrated master schedule for the overhaul's first phase, just 11,389 individual project schedules that are "not integrated," with installations at the same sites that risk disrupting controller operations. [5] The FAA also moved its copper-to-fiber deadline up by 21 months, from September 2030 to December 2028. [5] Speeding up a project while not having a master schedule is, technically, a strategy. It's the strategy of a man assembling IKEA furniture while it's on fire.

## So What Would Actually Fix It?

Here's the frustrating part: the fixes are not secret, and some of the people yelling at each other agree on them.

**Spend the money that already exists, fast, and show your work.** House Democrats say $11 billion is unspent; [6] the administration says that money was earmarked for other parts of the job. [3] Fine. Publish exactly what's obligated, where, and when. Bedford is expected to face questions at an early December hearing. [6] That's a good place to start.

**Do what GAO said.** Build a reliable lifecycle cost estimate and a real integrated master schedule. GAO recommended both; the Transportation Department only partially agreed. [5] When the auditors tell you that 11,389 schedules is not a schedule, the correct response is not "partially."

**Fund it the way the president, of all people, described.** Trump said the work should be done "all at once, not in drips and drabs." [8] He's right. Multi-year, protected funding that doesn't vanish every time Congress plays chicken with a shutdown would be the single most boring and most effective thing Washington could do for air travel. When the 2025 shutdown forced flight cuts at 40 airports, [11] that was the bill for doing it the other way.

**Keep paying controllers, and keep hiring them.** Record hiring is good. [12] Not paying them during shutdowns is not.

**And maybe, just maybe, don't swap the plumbing at rush hour.**

Because the next time this happens, and on current evidence there will be a next time, there will be another press conference, another number with a "B" after it, and another round of blaming whoever had the job last. The copper will still be from the 1960s. [5] And somewhere in southern Arkansas, a router that may or may not have done anything wrong will sit quietly in a lab, knowing it has been the most powerful object in American aviation. [4]

El Dorado was never a city of gold. It was a warning. Fix the wires.

pt.dek: Uma caixa em El Dorado, no Arkansas, pode ter parado todas as decolagens do país. Ela só conseguiu por causa de cobre dos anos 1960, dinheiro a conta-gotas e muita culpa jogada em quem estava antes no cargo.

de.title: Das Hauptthema: Ein Router legte Amerikas Flugverkehr lahm, und Washington hat ihn so verkabelt
de.dek: Ein Kasten in El Dorado, Arkansas, hat womöglich jeden Abflug im Land gestoppt. Möglich machten das Kupferkabel aus den 1960ern, Geld in Tropfen und viel Schuldzuweisung an den jeweiligen Vorgänger.
